children: "Further modest tightening" of monetary policy may be needed if economic conditions unfold as Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson expects, she said on Thursday.
The reason is that the Federal Reserve's benchmark interest rate doesn't appear to be lowering inflation that has remained above the central bank's 2% goal for more than five years.
"By September, it was clear that inflation risks were growing," she said in opening remarks at the Philly Fed's 10th Annual Fintech Conference. "Underlying inflation showed little to no progress."

Paulson, who votes on the Federal Open Market Committee this year, pointed to upward pricing pressures from tariffs and the AI buildout. At the same time, "economic growth firmed up a little, and the labor market strengthened a touch. Against this backdrop, the risk of persistently elevated inflation had increased."

"This recalibration brings policy closer to what I believe is needed to return inflation to 2% at a pace that appropriately balances inflation risks with risks to the labor market," she said. "Looking ahead, if conditions evolve as I expect, some modest further tightening may be warranted."

The Philly Fed president said she'll continue to watch the data and will closely listen to what businesses and workers are telling her. "But let me be clear: returning inflation to 2 percent is non-negotiable, and I will support the policy path that gets us there while carefully weighing risks to the labor market along the way," she said.
